Neonates of Mahi-mahi (Coryphaena hippurus) emerge from the egg at a total length at birth of just 0.5 centimeters [Lb = 0.5 centimeters], a diminutive size reflecting the pelagic larval strategy characteristic of this species. Following hatch, the prolarvae remain lecithotrophic for a brief period, with the transition to exogenous feeding occurring quickly. The age at birth is approximately 1.7 days [ab = approximately 1.7 days] when maintained at a constant temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a thermal regime that promotes rapid early development. During this initial phase, the yolk-sac larva depends entirely on endogenous reserves. The prolonged incubation period relative to some other scombrid-like teleosts is likely linked to the relatively large egg size and substantial yolk volume, which support a relatively developed hatchling. The larval period is marked by an exceptional growth velocity under these warm, food-rich conditions. Field-reared individuals sampled from pelagic nurseries routinely exhibit a total length at 15 days of around 1.5 centimeters  when water temperatures average 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This rapid elongation during the first fortnight lays the foundation for the species’ extraordinarily fast life history and its ability to reach large ultimate sizes within a single year.

By the time they reach 30 days post-hatching, Mahi-mahi larvae have more than doubled their length from the 15-day mark, with a total length at 30 days of 3 centimeters  under stable conditions at 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This measurement corresponds to the late larval or early flexion stage, when the notochord begins to upturn and fin rays start to ossify. The transition through larval metamorphosis is a critical developmental bottleneck; metamorphosis itself typically occurs when the fish attains a total length at metamorphosis of about 2 centimeters . At this point, the body plan reorganizes dramatically, with the transparent, planktonic larva transforming into a more robust, scaled, and pigmented juvenile capable of sustained swimming and pursuit predation. The duration of the pelagic larval phase is remarkably short for a fish reaching such a large adult body size, a trait that enables Mahi-mahi to exploit ephemeral, high-productivity habitats. Following settlement into the near-surface pelagic zone, the young juveniles disperse widely, tracking warm-water currents and aggregating under floating objects. Their rapid elongation and ability to feed on a wide range of zooplankton and small nekton during this stage underpins the species’ capacity to grow from a 0.5 cm hatchling to a 3 cm individual in just one month.

The adult body size of Mahi-mahi is among the largest of any pelagic teleost reaching sexual maturity within its first year, with the ultimate fork length frequently exceeding 210 centimeters [Li = 210 centimeters] in both sexes, though males typically attain slightly larger maximum dimensions. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for the largest individuals is approximately 39,500 grams (39500 grams) [Wwi = 39500 grams], a value consistent with the 40-kilogram maximum recorded by FishBase. This impressive size is a product of sustained, near-exponential growth throughout the juvenile and sub-adult stages. First reproduction, defined by the first successful spawning event, occurs when females reach a total length at puberty of approximately 20 centimeters [Lp = approximately 20 centimeters]. The age at first reproduction is estimated at around 137 days after hatching [tR = around 137 days after hatching] when water temperatures are held at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], a remarkably brief maturation period. This trait classifies Mahi-mahi as an extreme example of an r-selected, fast-growing predator, contrasting sharply with other large-bodied pelagic fishes like tunas and billfishes that require several years to become reproductively active.

Reproductive output in Mahi-mahi is prodigious, reflecting the high mortality rates experienced during the early life stages. A single, large, sexually mature female can release a maximum daily reproduction rate of approximately 5,479 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 5,479 eggs per day] when acclimated to 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. This staggering output is partitioned across multiple, frequent spawning events during the extended breeding season in tropical and subtropical waters. Specifically, each batch contains approximately 5,479 eggs [N_R_i = approximately 5,479 eggs] per individual spawning event, and a female may spawn once per day [F_R_i = once per day] throughout the warm season. The eggs are small, transparent, and pelagic, drifting in the surface plankton until hatching. This high-frequency, high-volume spawning strategy compensates for intense egg and larval predation and allows Mahi-mahi to rapidly colonize favorable oceanographic features such as drift lines and convergence zones. The energetic cost of such sustained gamete production is immense, requiring continuous high feeding rates on squid, flying fish, and other pelagic prey.

The lifespan of wild Mahi-mahi is short relative to other large pelagic fishes, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 5 years [am = approximately 5 years] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Most individuals in exploited populations live no more than 2 to 3 years, however, given intense fishing pressure. This compressed lifespan is coupled with a physiological trajectory that prioritizes rapid growth and early, high-investment reproduction over somatic longevity. The species is iteroparous, meaning individuals can spawn repeatedly over successive breeding seasons, but the majority of lifetime reproductive output is concentrated in the first year or two of life. Natural death occurs primarily through predation by larger tunas, billfish, and sharks, although senescent individuals become increasingly vulnerable to disease and starvation as they approach their 5-year maximum age (5 years) [am = 5 years] at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. Comparative studies within the family Coryphaenidae underscore that this life-history syndrome—extremely fast growth, early maturation, high fecundity, and a short maximum lifespan—is a direct adaptation to the ephemeral, high-mortality environment of the open ocean surface waters that Mahi-mahi inhabits.
